idiom_name: when expression over a sealed interface or enum (compiler-checked exhaustiveness)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's when over a sealed class or interface is exhaustive by construction: the compiler checks that all direct non-sealed subtypes are covered (and that every enum entry is handled), so no else branch is needed and a new subtype breaks every when that must handle it. Non-exhaustive when on a sealed type was made a warning for statements in 1.6 and an error in 1.7, matching the long-standing rule for when used as an expression. Smart casts inside is branches remove the casts the classic structure needs, and sealed interfaces (since 1.5) let the sealed declaration and its variants live in one module; add else only for genuinely open subjects, where it trades the compile-time proof away.
pitfalls: An else branch removes the check: the compiler stops proving coverage, so new subtypes are caught only by tests.
In multiplatform common code an else is still required for expect sealed hierarchies, because actual subtypes are unknown there - another quiet way to lose the guarantee.
Exhaustiveness is only checked for sealed, enum and Boolean subjects; when over String or Int is a plain comparison chain with no coverage analysis.
